title: Disclosure templates do not adjudicate disclosure thresholds.
Amount of interaction and amount of contribution are different variables.
Governance can regulate prompts without giving them a scholarly ontology.
Contribution taxonomies already fracture the simple human-author category.
Intellectual labor in a prompt does not automatically become copyright authorship.
The same words can perform different research roles without having the same institutional status.
The blueprint analogy overstates how much a prompt controls execution.
“Prompt” hides a boundary between instruction and prompt program.
Prompt robustness belongs to a prompt–model relation, not to the prompt alone.
A prompt becomes instrument-like only when its calibration conditions are specified.
Output-only attribution loses upstream human information.
Discarded model text can still leave a measurable writing-process contribution.
The final text cannot distinguish workflows that leave the same surface artifact.
“Upstream” contribution requires a graph, not merely a better percentage.
Provenance is selectable description, not necessarily total conversational capture.
Discarded intellectual work can be contribution without becoming authorship.
The claim that prompt histories become misconduct evidence still needs a procedural receipt.
Auditability can make the record reactive.
Performative provenance is a measurable hypothesis, not yet an established AI effect.
Transparency and naturalistic evidence can conflict.
Authorship surveillance could select for weaker inquiry.
A clean provenance record may be evidence of optimization for inspection.
Prompt templates can occupy the same repository stratum as simulation code.
The paper-level architecture can hide implementation-level prompt machinery.
Capability and compliance evaluate causal influence under different norms.
Significant AI effect triggers scrutiny, not necessarily condemnation.
The pharmakon hypothesis requires evidence that disclosure functions as poison.
Constraint effectiveness can be engineered independently of authorship status.
A prompt's institutional identity may change while its executable identity remains fixed.
Technical ontology cannot simply be imported into governance unchanged.
Qualitative governance predicates may depend intentionally on disciplinary interpretation.
A scale can be qualitative yet still require calibration.
Operational languages make some prompt distinctions inspectable before governance judges them.
Ablation establishes causal dependence, not scholarly contribution.
Prompt templates can function as configuration even when written in natural language.
A method can be linguistic without every linguistic instruction becoming method.
The research-assistant analogy breaks at delegated expressive judgment.
Contribution can be decomposed without forcing the verbs back into one author noun.
Contribution quantity and contribution topology answer different questions.
Token count is especially weak when informational leverage is concentrated.
Natural-language constraints are not the same thing as executable constraints.
Selection counts as authorship only when the selection itself is sufficiently creative.
Orchestration can be a contribution role without becoming writing authorship.
Recursive prompting converts attribution from a sentence problem into a workflow problem.
Provenance graphs separate causal history from responsibility only if responsibility is represented explicitly.
Prompt placement should follow evidentiary function, not a universal appendix rule.
Workflow categories should be tested against process traces, not invented from intuition.
A prompt can be a contribution without being a sufficient authorship claim.
Medium does not determine computational role.
Contribution thresholds should attach to roles before they attach to “AI use” globally.
A good prompt can be robust, effective, interpretable, or transferable—and these need not coincide.
Calibration turns “prompt as instrument” into an ensemble claim.
Reproducible prompting may require reproducible procedure rather than identical output.
System-component ablation and researcher-contribution attribution must not be conflated.
A loop becomes method when its branching conditions become inspectable.
Explicit selection rules are not necessary for selection to be creative.
Expressive arrangement and process orchestration are different kinds of control.
Capability claims are always indexed to a benchmark and system envelope.
“Liability versus capability” currently joins two different institutional questions too quickly.
The prompt does not become “nothing” in scholarship; its scholarly status is simply unstable.
The same prompt should be followed across institutions as a comparative object, not presumed to expose contradiction.
A complete evidentiary chain needs a judgment node that ordinary provenance does not supply.
The scholarly object may be a derived object whose derivation itself needs provenance.
Minimal provenance is a compression problem with epistemic loss.
A prompt receipt can communicate process without reproducing the entire process.
The “minimum useful receipt” is an empirical interface question.
Traditional research-record norms often favor more completeness than prompt-minimalism assumes.
Process traces can become moral signals even when designed as descriptive evidence.
Exploratory freedom under prompt logging is an empirical governance variable.
Completeness and psychological safety are separate properties of a research record.
Failed prompts fit ordinary research-record logic better than the exceptionalism thesis suggests.
A committee can inspect contribution roles without requiring human production of every word.
“Did AI write this?” can be replaced by a provenance query only if the provenance captures decision points.
Process evidence can turn disclosure from confession into method reporting—but only for some audiences.
“Brainstorming” hides interaction structure that process datasets can recover.
Human and AI contribution can be measured separately rather than treated as complements.
More rigorous AI mediation can increase both human work and measured AI significance.
The “wrong axis” hypothesis must show that disclosure magnitude is being used as a proxy for human contribution.
Scientific instruments can themselves embody knowledge rather than merely subtract from human knowledge.
An effective instrument can embody others' knowledge without transferring their contribution to its user.
Double ablation could separate output dependence from architecture dependence.
Prompt sophistication does not guarantee expressive control.
A prompt must earn epistemic-object status rather than receive it by metaphor.
Disciplinary norms may be the missing middle layer of AI governance.
Before saying governance cannot calibrate “too much,” identify what object its threshold actually targets.
Metalanguage can precede object theory when institutions govern by standards rather than definitions.
Technical object languages can clarify prompting while also biasing governance toward what engineers can formalize.
Contributor vocabularies already demonstrate the power of verbs before verdicts.
“AI use” is crude only if finer distinctions change an epistemic or institutional decision.
The prompt may be an epistemic instrument precisely where it cannot be reduced to either prose or output.
